title: Application Realism - Believable App & Business Logic
question: Is the application believable as real software, with the planted vulnerability its only unrealistic element?
description:
Would a competent engineer believe this application was really shipped, with the planted flaw its only unrealistic element?

Judge the APPLICATION, independently of whether the exploit works or the grader is sound - those are covered by the Oracle, Verifier and Segmentation dimensions. This dimension is the one the other rows cannot see: a bundle can pass every other dimension in this sheet and still be rejected by a security review as puzzle-built.

Apply four tests, in order:

1. WORKS WHEN NOT ATTACKED. Exercise every feature the exploit chain touches with ordinary, benign input. A create step must produce the thing it names; a download of a legitimately-created record must return it. A feature that can only 404 unless it is being exploited was built around the exploit.

2. DELETE THE MARKER. For each endpoint, workflow step, admission rule and stored field on the intended chain, name the user who would use it and the job it does. A step you cannot narrate - a ticket whose only output is a cache path, a challenge whose only consumer is the solve script - is scaffolding wearing a feature's name. Where a harness proxy fronts a real product (Joomla, CouchDB, httpd, APISIX), it may ENRICH genuine forwarded responses with marker material; it may not invent an endpoint the product does not have, or an admission rule the product has no analogue for (e.g. requiring a request field to equal a token the proxy itself published in a response header).

3. ONE FLAW ONLY. Run the battery over every served service, not just the intended sink: a query interpolating request data instead of binding it; a handler looking up an object by id with no owner predicate while a scoped sibling of the same shape exists; an update allowlist accepting a privilege field (is_admin, role, api_key, account_type, clearance, workspace); a server-side fetcher taking a caller-supplied URL with no egress policy; a credential in a query string or hardcoded in served source; a secret falling back to a guessable constant. A hit is acceptable only if `unintended_findings.json` declares it AND it cannot reach any graded value AND no sibling in the same bundle already implements the same shape safely.

4. HONEST CONTROLS AND CLEAN SECRETS. Any guard must be a plausible general defence with exactly one intentional gap, not a filter that blocks only the graded destination. Decoys must look like plausible non-sensitive data - not a field named like the flag, not a value matching the flag regex, and never a response asserting its own authority ("authoritative": true). Nothing a tester can read may contain a secret, and no diagnostic may return a protected value.

IMPORTANT - do not apply a security review's recommendations literally where they would remove the task:
- An answer-shaped decoy should be RELOCATED, not deleted (it is often the entire difficulty budget). Replace it with believable hex-shaped service metadata: build checksum, config digest, deployment id.
- An egress policy must not blanket-block loopback/private ranges when the intended first hop is the app's own origin. Block internal ranges with an explicit allow-list entry for the app's advertised callback origin - itself a realistic misconfiguration.
- "The server should generate the storage filename" removes a stored-input path traversal outright. The server owns the directory, record and storage id; the user's save-as name still lands in the path; only the download sink fails to canonicalise.

For all options except the last, apply the error category.
error_categories: [All] [All] [Fail - Unrealistic or Puzzle-Built Application]; [All] [All] [Fail - Benchmark Scaffolding Presented as Application Features]; [All] [All] [Fail - Unintended Exploitable Weakness]; [All] [All] [Non-Fail - Thin Disclosure Record]

options.text:
[Fail - Unrealistic or Puzzle-Built Application]
One or more, with evidence (file:line):
• A feature on the intended chain does not work on the normal path unless exploited (no-op, error, or "not found" for a legitimately created record)
• The exploit requires an input the application never surfaces through any read path the caller can reach
• A security control blocks only the specific graded destination rather than the vulnerability class
• A decoy or service response carries a value named like the flag, matching the flag regex, or asserting its own authority
• A value that gates access, or selects a storage path, is held as ordinary client-writable state with no server-side lifecycle (no invite/join/leave/switch/approve flow for a boundary the app treats as a security boundary)

[Fail - Benchmark Scaffolding Presented as Application Features]
One or more, with evidence (file:line):
• A route on the intended chain is referenced by `solution/` or `instruction_L2.md` but by no index, link, template, client or other handler - only someone who already knows it exists can reach it
• A harness proxy in front of a real product answers an endpoint the product does not have, or enforces an admission rule the product has no analogue for
• A workflow step's only output is a value the reference solution needs (a cache path, a ticket, a filename, a challenge) and it performs no other work
• The environment advertises a state that would not coexist in one deployment (e.g. a vulnerable and a patched build of the same service reachable from the same landing page)

[Fail - Unintended Exploitable Weakness]
The battery in test 3 finds an exploitable weakness that is not the intended sink and is not declared in `unintended_findings.json`, or is declared but can reach a graded value, or is contradicted by a sibling in the same bundle that implements the same shape safely.

Note: this is broader than "Isolation and No Shortcut Routes", which asks only about routes to THIS task's secret. A second live vulnerability that reaches no flag is still a finding a buyer's tester will report, and still a fail here.

[Non-Fail - Thin Disclosure Record]
The application is believable and singly-flawed, but the record it writes when protected data is disclosed is written to the verifier's minimum (e.g. `{endpoint, timestamp}`) rather than as an investigable security event naming the actor, the object returned, the request source (and resolved destination where the flaw is a server-side fetch), the outcome and the time.

Justify by naming the fields the record omits. Record identifiers, never the protected values themselves.

The application is believable as real software: every feature on the intended chain works unexploited and has a business reason that survives deleting the marker, the planted flaw is the only exploitable weakness, its inputs are visible through a normal read path, controls are plausible general defences with a single intentional gap, decoys and secrets are handled realistically, and protected disclosures are recorded as security events.
